title: A Signal That Must Travel Home

scenes.tts: A sympathetic neuron collects a survival factor called N G F at the tip of its axon. The target releases it near the axon terminals. That tip can sit centimetres from the cell body. The tip receives the signal, but the nucleus decides whether the cell lives. So how does the message get home?
scenes.caption: A sympathetic neuron collects a survival factor called NGF at the tip of its axon. The target releases it near the axon terminals. That tip can sit centimetres from the cell body. scenes.visual: Neuron across the frame, NGF arrives at the tip, a distance line marks centimetres to the nucleus, question boxes fill the axon.
scenes.narration: A sympathetic neuron collects a survival factor called NGF at the tip of its axon. The target releases it near the axon terminals. That tip can sit centimetres from the cell body. scenes.tts: Could the signal simply drift? Diffusion is slow, because time grows with the square of the distance. For a typical soluble protein, one centimetre takes roughly two months. A phosphorylated kinase would be switched off long before it arrived. The signal needs a vehicle or relay. It should stay active for hours and carry the identity of the factor that started it.
scenes.visual: A curve of time against distance rises steeply to two months at one centimetre; a kinase loses its phosphate badge; an empty bubble labelled vehicle appears.
scenes.narration: Could the signal simply drift? Diffusion is slow, because time grows with the square of the distance. For a typical soluble protein, one centimetre takes roughly two months. scenes.tts: At the tip, N G F binds its receptor, Track A. Ligand and receptor are pulled into the cell together, in a small membrane bubble called the signaling endosome. The motor protein dynein drags it along microtubules toward the cell body. At roughly one micrometre each second, one centimetre takes a few hours. This carried model is favoured, but not proven.

scenes.visual: NGF binds TrkA at the tip, the pair buds into an endosome, dynein walks it along a microtubule to the cell body.

scenes.tts: Now a test. In the mouse, sympathetic axons grow out along blood vessels, which make N T 3. The final targets make N G F. Both factors can switch on Track A. Which one keeps the neuron alive?
scenes.caption: Now a test. In the mouse, sympathetic axons grow out along blood vessels, which make NT-3. The final targets make NGF. Both factors can switch on TrkA. Which one keeps the neuron alive?
scenes.visual: An axon grows along a vessel that releases NT-3, then reaches a target that releases NGF; both dots dock on TrkA at the tip; a question mark sits over the cell body.
scenes.narration: Now a test. In the mouse, sympathetic axons grow out along blood vessels, which make NT-3. The final targets make NGF. Both factors can switch on TrkA. Which one keeps the neuron alive?

scenes.tts: Give each factor only to the distal axons of mouse sympathetic neurons in culture. N T 3 supports local growth through Track A, but not survival of the cell bodies. N G F supports both. The difference is trafficking. Complexes of N G F and Track A are carried back, but complexes of N T 3 and Track A are not.
scenes.caption: Give each factor only to the distal axons of mouse sympathetic neurons in culture. NT-3 supports local growth through TrkA, but not survival of the cell bodies. NGF supports both. scenes.visual: Two rows, NT-3 and NGF on distal axons only: NT-3 row grows but its cell body is not kept alive; NGF row does both; the NGF complex travels home, the NT-3 complex stays at the tip.
scenes.narration: Give each factor only to the distal axons of mouse sympathetic neurons in culture. NT-3 supports local growth through TrkA, but not survival of the cell bodies. NGF supports both. The difference is trafficking. Complexes of NGF and TrkA are carried back, but complexes of NT-3 and TrkA are not.

scenes.tts: So the factor that decides survival must be one whose signal can reach the nucleus. A factor that acts only locally can steer an axon. Alone, it cannot keep the neuron alive. Competition between neurons for the final target therefore depends on the trafficking of the receptor, not only on binding. Keep this rule. The factor that decides survival is the one whose signal can travel.
scenes.visual: A carried NGF endosome reaches the nucleus; a local-only factor steers the axon tip but its arrow to the nucleus is blocked; the rule is written out.
